# Pull requests

The deep dive for principle 6 of [[git-workflow]] — a PR is reviewed, a diff is not. This is the size, shape, description, and review etiquette that makes the review-and-ship loop actually work.

## PR size

The empirical research keeps converging on the same number: review effectiveness falls off a cliff somewhere around **400 lines of meaningful diff**. Above that, reviewers skim. Above 1000, they stop reading.

"Meaningful" excludes:
- Generated files (lockfiles, snapshot files, build outputs).
- Pure renames or moves (track these as their own commit so they're easy to skip in review).
- Vendored / autogenerated code.

Most reviewers can carefully read **300–400 changed lines** in 30 minutes. If your PR is two or three multiples of that, expect the review to be one of:
- An "LGTM" four minutes after open (didn't read it; the bug ships).
- Indefinite stalling because nobody has a free 90-minute block to read it (the branch rots).
- A surface review of one of the changes; the other changes go uninspected.

When a PR has to be large (a real refactor, a vendor migration), say so explicitly in the description and call out which sections actually need careful eyes vs which are mechanical.

## Description template

Every PR — yes, every one — gets a description. The template:

```markdown
## Summary
- [2–4 bullets describing what changed at the behavior or shape level]

## Why
[The motivation. The constraint. The linked issue. The trade-off considered.
This is the most valuable part of the PR; it's what the future bisecter will read.]

## Test plan
- [ ] [Concrete check the reviewer can re-run]
- [ ] [Another one]
- [ ] [Edge case you specifically thought about]

## Notes for reviewer (optional)
[Any context the diff doesn't carry: deploy order, feature-flag state, anything
that needs to happen alongside merging.]

## Screenshots / examples (for UI or API changes)
[Before / after. Request / response. Whatever the change is best demonstrated as.]
```

**What to put in each section:**

- **Summary** — say what the code now does that it didn't before, at the level a teammate cares about. "Adds user_id column to audit rows" beats "Modifies AuditEntry struct and 3 callers."
- **Why** — the part that doesn't survive in the code. Compliance requirement? Specific incident? Performance problem? Engineering decision over the alternative? Write it down.
- **Test plan** — checkable items, not "I tested it." The reviewer should be able to walk down the list and reproduce. For backend changes, that often means `curl` invocations or test names. For UI, click paths.
- **Screenshots** — for any UI change. A 2-second screenshot saves the reviewer from spinning up the app.

This project's `/dev` flow auto-generates a description close to this shape, pulling the *what* from `spec.md` and the *how-verified* from `tests.md`. The engineer agent can lift the spec's acceptance scenarios (`AC#`) directly into the test-plan checkboxes.

## Draft vs ready

Open a PR as **Draft** the moment you have something to push — even if it's incomplete. Benefits:
- CI runs early; you find broken tests before review starts.
- The PR URL exists for cross-linking.
- It signals to teammates "this is in flight" so they can avoid touching the same files.
- It costs nothing — drafts don't appear in review queues.

Flip from Draft → Ready only when:
- CI is green.
- You've self-reviewed the diff at least once. (`git diff main...HEAD` and read every line.)
- The description is complete.
- You'd be comfortable with someone merging it as-is.

**Don't** request review on a red PR or a PR with TODOs in the diff. It teaches reviewers to ignore CI ("they always request review while CI runs") and to skim past TODOs ("they always say they'll fix later"). Both habits cost you when you actually need a careful review.

## Splitting a big PR

If your PR is past ~600 lines, consider splitting. Common splits:

- **Refactor + feature** → ship the refactor first as its own PR. It's mechanical, fast to review, and reduces the feature PR's diff. The feature PR then carries only behavior changes.
- **Migration + use of migration** → ship the schema migration alone first (expand). Then add the feature that reads or writes the new column. Lets you roll back the feature without rolling back the schema.
- **Big rename + everything else** → ship the rename alone. Reviewers can re-run the tool and confirm correctness in seconds; the actual behavior change is then reviewable on its own.
- **Vendored update + adaptation** → ship the vendor bump in one PR (or one commit clearly marked). Adaptations live separately.

The mechanism for splitting: see [stacked PRs](#stacked-prs).

## Stacked PRs

A stack is two or more PRs where each depends on the previous: PR-A merges to `main`, then PR-B (branched from A) merges to `main`. While both are open, B's diff shown against `main` includes A's changes too — confusing for reviewers. Two ways to handle it:

1. **Change the base branch.** Set PR-B's base to A's branch (most platforms support this). The diff now shows only B's changes. When A merges, the platform auto-redirects B to `main`.
2. **Wait for A to merge.** If the work is genuinely sequential and not parallelizable, just review and merge A first; then B opens normally against `main`.

When the stack is more than 2 deep or rebases get gnarly, tools like `ghstack`, `git-spr`, `git-branchless`, or Graphite's CLI help. But most stacks are 2–3 PRs deep — manual is fine.

Rebase the stack from the bottom up; see `references/branching-and-rebasing.md` for the mechanics.

## Responding to review comments

The author's etiquette:

- **Reply to every comment**, even if it's just to acknowledge. Silent dismissal feels disrespectful even when nothing's intended.
- **Use a "fixup" commit** for each round of changes, then squash before merge. Reviewers can see exactly what you changed in response to feedback; the final history stays clean.
- **Don't resolve a thread you didn't open.** If the reviewer raised it, let the reviewer close it. (You can mark it "addressed in <commit-sha>" and they'll close it.)
- **Push back when you disagree.** "I considered that, but X" is a real reply; quietly making the change you didn't believe in is worse than not making it.
- **Don't force-push during active review** if you can help it. Reviewers lose track of what changed since their last read. If you must (e.g., to rebase onto a hot `main` fix), drop a comment saying "rebased only, no logic changes" or "rebased plus addressed X."

The reviewer's etiquette:

- **One review pass = one round.** Submit comments as a batch, not as a stream of individual nits. Lets the author handle them as a unit.
- **Distinguish nits from blockers.** Prefix optional comments: `nit:`, `optional:`, `consider:`. Reviewer authority is real — be explicit about what you're asserting.
- **Approve when the bar is met, not when the diff is perfect.** "I'd write this differently" is not a blocker; "this has a bug" is.
- **Ask, don't assume.** "What happens when X is null?" beats "Crashes on X=null, fix." You may be wrong.

## AI-assisted review

AI reviewers (GitHub Copilot's PR review, CodeRabbit, Greptile, the various Claude/Cursor integrations) are now table-stakes for many teams — useful as a *first-pass* on a PR to catch mechanical issues, naming inconsistencies, missing tests for obvious branches, dead code, and surface-level security smells. Treat them as a fast pre-reviewer, not a substitute for human judgment.

**Rules of engagement:**

- **AI review never counts toward required approvals.** GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket all enforce this; mirror it in your own policy. Human accountability is the only kind that survives an incident postmortem.
- **AI catches mechanical issues; humans catch *fit*.** Whether the change matches the system's intent, whether the boundary is in the right place, whether the test coverage exercises the actual risk — these are human-review jobs that AI is still poor at.
- **Read AI comments like a junior reviewer's.** Often correct, sometimes confidently wrong (especially when it lacks the surrounding context — e.g., it doesn't know that the "missing null check" is enforced upstream). Don't blindly action them; push back the same way you would on a colleague.
- **Don't let AI-review turn into a discussion partner.** If you find yourself replying to an AI comment to *explain* the design, the explanation belongs in the PR description or a code comment — not buried in a review thread.

Good division of labor: AI handles the "have you considered…" mechanical surface; humans handle the "is this the right design and does it match what the system needs" question. PRs reviewed only by AI are not reviewed.

## Merging

Three options:

- **Squash merge** (the most common default). The branch's commits collapse into one commit on `main`. Pros: linear `main` log, no half-baked WIP commits ever land. Cons: loses the granularity (the carefully-crafted atomic commits become one); some teams care, others don't.
- **Merge commit** (preserves branch). All branch commits land as-is, with a merge commit tying them in. Pros: keeps the atomic commit granularity. Cons: `main` log is noisier; bisect has to navigate a graph.
- **Rebase merge** (no merge commit). Branch commits replay onto `main` linearly. Pros: linear, preserves granularity. Cons: rewrites the SHAs of the branch (so post-merge branches that reference these commits become orphans).

This project doesn't enforce a single choice — pick what fits your team. The `/dev` flow's commits are designed to be atomic and well-messaged, which means *any* of the three works (squash is wasteful of the granularity; rebase or merge-commit both preserve it). If your team squashes, ensure the squash commit's message is hand-edited to summarize, not just concatenate.

**One rule regardless of strategy:** never merge a red PR. Re-running the merge to "see if it goes green this time" is a tell that someone is about to ship a bug.
